extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative dimensions for providing ready-to-use, newsworthy information (information subsidies) — typically press releases, press seminars, and conferences — to news media, and for assessing their effects on news production and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of ready-to-use newsworthy information
rubrics_metrics.description: An information subsidy is the provision of ready-to-use newsworthy information to the news media by various sources interested in gaining access to media time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials should be prepared so they are newsworthy and immediately usable by journalists; the aim is to gain access to media time and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical forms / formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical forms of information subsidies include press releases, as well as press seminars and conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases, press seminars, and conferences are standard vehicles for delivering information subsidies; choose the form appropriate to the message and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style and format (easy incorporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information presented in a format (such as an inverted pyramid) and style that can be easily incorporated in news is more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use journalistic-friendly structures (e.g., inverted pyramid), clear lead facts, and concise copy so journalists can quickly incorporate content into stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic efficiency / cost-reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Information subsidies represent a subsidy to the media, since they lower the cost of news-gathering and shorten the time to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing ready-to-use material reduces reporters' resource burden compared with alternatives (investigative work, informal channels, routine sources), making the subsidy attractive to news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitorability and maintainability (routine sourcing advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of alternatives available to the media to collect information — investigative work, informal channels and routine sources — the latter channel (information subsidies) is the cheapest to monitor and maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, routinized information subsidies are easier and cheaper for newsrooms to track over time than ad hoc investigative efforts or informal networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for bias in subsidised materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The subsidised materials are usually biased in favour of the source organisation; from the source's point of view, the ideal goal is to have the news media view reflect as closely as possible their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should be aware that their materials are perceived as source-biased; journalists should treat such materials critically and verify claims rather than reproduce them verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of skewing news selection and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue that subsidies have the potential to skew the process of news selection by leading journalists to pick stories based on criteria other than their inherent importance and newsworthiness; the content of coverage is also likely to be influenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether reliance on subsidies causes disproportionate coverage of subsidiser-favored topics or frames; consider balancing with independent reporting and editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between accessibility and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on information provided by external sources can relieve the economic burden and shorten publication time, but may compromise editorial independence and the intrinsic newsworthiness criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both producers and newsrooms should weigh the benefits of accessibility and speed against the need for independent verification and editorial criteria of importance.
